name: Dana Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Dana. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Our crew covers the farm country north of Hollins, a lot of long single-phase lines down gravel roads to farms and grain bins. I'm the ground hand, so I'm the one with the chainsaw clearing branches off the lines, digging, hauling the cross-arms and keeping the truck stocked. We start at seven from the co-op yard, say a short prayer if Earl's leading the safety talk, and head out. I love being out in the fields I grew up in, and the farmers know me, so I get a coffee at half the stops. What wears me out is the cold in January and feeling slow next to the young men.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been doing it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Three years. We had a dairy farm, Glen's family's for three generations, and in 2022 we had to sell it to clear the debts. I was fifty-five and needed a job with health cover, and the power company was hiring ground hands. Glen drives a grain truck in harvest season and does odd jobs the rest of the year, so it's my wage that keeps the lights on, funnily enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's go through five pictures of the future. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so. I never believed half of what they said about it on the news. At church I'd say the Lord gave us hands for a reason.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It wouldn't change a thing for me. I don't use those AI things, I've got a flip phone, and out on these roads nobody's going to send a computer to cut branches. I'd just keep on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going to work, keep my head down, and try to get my pole-climbing certificate by spring. We'd keep the budget tight, like always since the farm. Maybe we'd finally get the truck's brakes done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Relieved, really, that the world isn't turning upside down again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said again. What was the first time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Selling the farm. Glen's father milked those cows, and his father before him, and we signed it away at the kitchen table to a man from the city who'd never seen a cow give birth. That was the world turning upside down, and it wasn't a computer that did it, it was the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does money look like for you right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight but honest. My wage covers the rent on the house in town and the bills, Glen's harvest money covers the truck and the extras, and the church helps at Christmas if we're short, which I hate but accept. We've got maybe two weeks of money in the bank, if nothing breaks.

S0.say: I told you so, because she never believed half of what the news said about AI. At church she would say the Lord gave people hands for a reason.
S0.think: Nothing would change for her: she has a flip phone, never uses AI, and nobody will send a computer to cut branches off rural lines. She would just keep on.
S0.do: Keeps working and aims for her pole-climbing certificate by spring. Keeps the household budget tight and maybe gets the truck's brakes fixed.
S0.feel: Calm and relieved that the world isn't turning upside down again.
S0.quote: We signed it away at the kitchen table to a man from the city who'd never seen a cow give birth.
S0.fieldNote: Dana's sense of upheaval is rooted in losing her family's dairy farm to debt, which she blames on the bank. Faith and community are central, and she accepts church help even though she dislikes it. Without AI change, she feels calm and grounded.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the city people's problem, mostly, and out here we'll carry on. At church I'd say we'll look after our own. I'm not online, so that's that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd worry a bit. If they bring drones to check the lines, that's walking patrols gone, and that's my winter work. But I don't think they'll get a robot to cut branches on a gravel road anytime soon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait and see what the company does, and keep working. If they offered training on the new gadgets, I'd go if I had to, but I wouldn't volunteer. I'd talk to Pastor Mike about whether the church could help with a jobs list for people who get let go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit. Not scared yet, but watchful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd go to training if you had to. Why not volunteer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm fifty-eight and I've got enough to learn just getting up a pole. My head's full. Let the young ones do the gadgets; I'll do the work that needs a pair of boots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if jobs started going?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big tech companies, and the people who think everything can be done from a screen in the city. Not the power company so much; they've been fair to me. And not my crew, they're good men.

S1.say: It's mostly the city people's problem, and out in the country they'll carry on. At church she would say the community looks after its own.
S1.think: She worries a little that drones could take her winter patrol work. But she doesn't think a robot will cut branches on gravel roads anytime soon.
S1.do: Waits to see what the company does and keeps working. Goes to training only if required, and asks her pastor about a church jobs list for anyone laid off.
S1.feel: Uneasy and watchful, but not scared yet.
S1.quote: Let the young ones do the gadgets; I'll do the work that needs a pair of boots.
S1.fieldNote: Dana's first instinct is to wait and rely on community, not technology. She blames big tech and screen-based city thinking, but speaks loyally of her employer and crew. Her resistance to learning new tools is partly pride and partly exhaustion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's wrong and God didn't make us to sit idle. At church I'd be praying for everyone. I'd want our representatives to put a stop to it, or at least slow it down, and I'd vote for whoever said they would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years and I'm sixty. If robots can do line work by 2028, I've got nothing, no farm, no savings, no other jobs around Hollins. Glen's grain truck would be gone too, I'd bet, because they're already talking about self-driving trucks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything: no extras, sell Glen's old hunting rifle, maybe move in with our daughter on her farm if they'd have us. I'd lean on the church and family before any government program. And I'd write to our representative, which I've never done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, I won't lie. But I'd still believe the Lord has a plan, even if I can't see it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said family before government. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because family knows you and doesn't make you fill out forty pages. My mother always said a handout from a stranger costs you more than it gives. If it came to it, I'd take the help, but it'd be the last thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything the two years of warning would let you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pray more, honestly, and pay off the little we owe on the truck. Talk to our daughter early about the spare room. Beyond that, two years is nothing; you can't build a life in two years.

S2.say: It's wrong, and God didn't make people to sit idle. She would pray for everyone and vote for representatives who promise to stop it or slow it down.
S2.think: At sixty she would have nothing, with no farm, no savings and no other jobs near Hollins. Her husband's grain truck work would likely go too with self-driving trucks.
S2.do: Cuts all extras, sells her husband's old hunting rifle and asks to move in with their daughter on her farm. Leans on church and family before any government help and writes to her representative for the first time.
S2.feel: Frightened, but still trusting that the Lord has a plan.
S2.quote: My mother always said a handout from a stranger costs you more than it gives.
S2.fieldNote: Dana's fear is real but softened by faith, which keeps her from feeling completely out of options. She would turn to church and family first and government last. Her political action would be voting and writing to her representative, not protesting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a bit more fair, but it's still wrong. At church I'd say we need to look after each other. I'd still vote for anyone promising to slow it down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years and I'm sixty-three. I might just make it to retirement, if the company keeps us on till then. I'd still be worried sick about Glen and the kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get my certificate and work as long as they'd have me, every overtime shift. I'd try to save a bit, maybe fifty a month, which isn't much but it's something. I'd talk to our daughter about her farm, because if robots take over farm work too, she's in trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but there's hope. I can see the end of the road from here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your daughter about her farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her not to borrow for any new machinery, not now. We lost our farm because of debt, and I don't want her to go the same way. She'd say, Mom, it's not 1985, and I'd say, debt is debt in any year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd work every overtime shift. How's your body holding up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not great. My knees ache in the morning, and my shoulder's been sore since I hauled that reel last autumn. But I've worked through worse on the farm, calving in the snow at three in the morning.

S3.say: Five years is a bit fairer, but it's still wrong. She would tell her church to look after one another and still vote for anyone promising to slow it down.
S3.think: At sixty-three she might just reach retirement if the company keeps her on. She would still be worried sick about her husband and children.
S3.do: Gets her climbing certificate, works every overtime shift and saves about fifty a month. Warns her daughter not to borrow for new farm machinery.
S3.feel: Worried, but hopeful, able to see the end of the road.
S3.quote: She'd say, Mom, it's not 1985, and I'd say, debt is debt in any year.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives Dana a realistic path to retirement if she can keep working. Her advice to her daughter is shaped by losing the family farm to debt. She is pushing through physical pain, as she did on the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'll be retired by then, God willing. At church I'd say we need to get the young people ready. I'm not online, so nothing there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years and I'm sixty-eight, so I'd be done. My worry is our grandkids, and whether there'll be work for them out here. For me, I'd just be glad I made it through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working until I'm sixty-five, get the certificate, save what I can. I'd tell our grandson to learn a trade, a real one with his hands, and maybe something about fixing these robots. I'd keep up with church and family like always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, for the grandkids. For me, I'd feel mostly at peace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said learn a trade with his hands, and also fixing robots. Isn't that a contradiction?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a little. I don't trust these machines, but I know somebody has to fix them when they break, and they always break. Better my grandson than some fellow in an office a thousand miles away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell him, exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, Caleb, find the work that still needs a person to show up in the mud. And save your money, even when it's hard. And go to church, because when the world turns upside down, that's where you'll find your people.

S4.say: She'll be retired by then, God willing. At church she would say the young people need to be made ready.
S4.think: At sixty-eight she would be done working, and just glad she made it through. Her worry is whether there will be work for her grandchildren in the area.
S4.do: Keeps working until sixty-five, gets her certificate and saves what she can. Tells her grandson to learn a hands-on trade, possibly fixing robots, and keeps up church and family life.
S4.feel: Uneasy for the grandchildren, mostly at peace for herself.
S4.quote: Better my grandson than some fellow in an office a thousand miles away.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Dana feels at peace about her own future and shifts her worry to her grandchildren. She admits the contradiction in distrusting machines while advising her grandson to fix them. Her advice centres on hands-on work, saving and church community.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because there'd be no time and no farm to fall back on. What would help is if the company kept us older ones on until we could retire, and if churches and towns had a way to help folks find new work. I don't want money in the post; I want to be useful.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith, and that's what gets me through. When we lost the farm I sat in the back pew every Sunday for a year and didn't sing a note. I'm singing again now, and I'd like to keep singing whatever these machines do.

headlineQuote: When we lost the farm I sat in the back pew every Sunday for a year and didn't sing a note.
portrait: Dana Bauer is a 58-year-old ground hand on a rural distribution crew north of Hollins, who took the job after she and her husband Glen sold his family's dairy farm in 2022 to clear debts. Her wage keeps the household going, with Glen driving a grain truck at harvest, and they have about two weeks of savings. She has a flip phone, never uses AI, and relies on faith, church and family rather than government. She stays calm or watchful in the milder pictures, is frightened but steadied by faith in the 2028 picture, and sees a path to retirement with more time. Her deepest worries are for her daughter's farm and her grandchildren.
biggestWorry: The 2028 scenario, because there would be no time and no farm to fall back on.
whatWouldHelp: Her employer keeping older workers on until retirement, and churches and towns helping people find new work; she wants to be useful, not to get money in the post.
